Recent advances in neuroimaging have allowed researchers to observe brain activity during moral decision-making tasks. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies consistently demonstrate heightened activation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) when subjects evaluate moral dilemmas. Additionally, clinical observations of patients with vmPFC damage reveal pronounced impairments in moral reasoning, often leading to socially inappropriate decisions. These convergent lines of evidence have led a prominent group of neuroscientists to argue that the vmPFC is the critical neural substrate for moral reasoning. They posit that moral decision-making constitutes a unique cognitive module, largely independent from and localized separately within the brain compared to general emotional processing or utilitarian calculation. This modular view suggests that moral judgments arise from dedicated neural circuitry centered on the vmPFC.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument advanced by the neuroscientists?
